title: Perfect, Progressive and Complex Aspectual Relationships
orientation: Earlier lessons introduced the main present and past constructions. This lesson examines the places where a short form-and-time chart stops being enough. In a maintenance report, has repaired and has been repairing do not make the same claim about completion. In an account of experience, have known for years and have been considering for weeks describe different kinds of situation. You will learn to examine the verb’s meaning, the reference point and the surrounding time expressions together. You will also distinguish the deadline in by Friday from continuation in until Friday, and explain the expectations carried by already and yet. Begin with the foundational comparison before opening the more technical discussion of situation aspect. Your aim is a defensible interpretation and an accurate original sentence, including recognition that some contexts permit more than one form.
outcomes: Build and analyse perfect-progressive auxiliary sequences.
Explain completion, continuing activity and recent-result interpretations without absolute claims.
Choose for, since, by and until according to the intended relationship.
Distinguish ordinary stative readings from dynamic uses of the same verb.
Use already, yet, just, lately and recently with appropriate context and register.

modules.title: Combining perfect and progressive viewpoints
modules.definition: Perfect constructions relate a situation to a later reference point; progressive constructions present a situation from within its development. They can combine, and neither construction alone tells the whole story about completion or present consequences.
foundation: Compare The technician has repaired the pump with The technician has been repairing the pump. In the first, the repair is presented as an achieved event relevant now. In the second, attention falls on the activity over a recent interval. The second sentence does not by itself say whether the pump is now repaired. Form a perfect with have plus a past participle, and a progressive with be plus an -ing form. Their combination is have been repairing: been is the participle of be, and repairing carries the progressive meaning. With a past reference point, change the finite auxiliary to had.
intermediate: Interpret the whole expression, including the verb and its object. She has written three reports presents three completed products. She has been writing reports presents a process, perhaps repeatedly, without specifying how many were completed. A perfect simple can also describe a continuing state: We have owned this shop for years. A perfect progressive can describe an activity that has just stopped: You look exhausted; have you been carrying boxes? The visible exhaustion is evidence for recent activity; it does not prove the person is still carrying anything while the question is asked.
advanced: The same contrast operates with a past viewpoint: By noon, they had repaired the roof presents the repair as achieved before noon, whereas They had been repairing the roof before the storm arrived describes earlier activity. A simple perfect does not necessarily promise a permanent result. The roof has been repaired does not rule out a new leak tomorrow. Conversely, ongoing activity can produce results without reaching an intended endpoint. Consider a wet floor after someone has been washing it. Ask separately whether an event occurred, whether its endpoint was reached, and which consequences the context makes relevant.
expert: Advanced analysis distinguishes grammatical aspect from the situation type expressed by the whole predicate. Write reports allows an open activity; write three reports supplies a countable endpoint. This interaction is sometimes called lexical aspect or situation aspect. Perfect progressive does not automatically mean a longer duration than perfect simple, nor is simple a guarantee of a short event. Both I have worked here for ten years and I have been working here for ten years can be appropriate; the latter puts greater attention on the activity or its continuing course. Translation and editing should preserve the intended viewpoint rather than mechanically substituting forms.

patterns.meaning: A perfect construction interpreted relative to now or another reference point.
Perfect and progressive meanings combine; completion must be inferred from the full context.

examples.sentence: The archivist has catalogued eighty letters.
examples.analysis: The stated total concerns completed cataloguing events.

examples.sentence: The archivist has been cataloguing letters all morning.
examples.analysis: The activity occupies a recent interval; the completed total is unspecified.

examples.sentence: The floor was slippery because someone had been washing it.
examples.analysis: Earlier washing explains a later past condition; washing need not still have been happening.

contrasts.b: I have been reading the chapter.
contrasts.note: Both are grammatical. The first normally presents completion of the chapter; the second highlights engagement in the activity and leaves completion open.

exceptions: An achievement verb can occur in a progressive when context supports repetition or an unfolding stage: The old engine has been stopping unexpectedly describes repeated stops, not one indefinitely extended instant.

mistakes.problem: She has been wrote the conclusion.
mistakes.repair: She has been writing the conclusion.
mistakes.reason: After progressive been, use the -ing form; wrote is a past-tense form.

mistakes.problem: They had been repaired the road before the rain; the intended subject is the repair crew.
mistakes.repair: They had been repairing the road before the rain.
mistakes.reason: The active perfect progressive requires repairing. They had repaired the road is another construction with a different presentation of completion.

glossary.definition: The temporal viewpoint relative to which another situation is interpreted.
glossary.example: In By noon, we had finished, noon supplies a past reference point.

glossary.definition: The temporal character of a predicate, including whether it expresses an endpoint.
glossary.example: Write a letter supplies an endpoint more explicitly than write letters.

modules.title: States, actions, temporary interpretations and repetition
modules.definition: Stative and dynamic describe interpretations of predicates. A stative reading presents a condition or relationship; a dynamic reading presents activity or change. Many verbs support more than one reading, and progressive compatibility depends on that reading and its context.
foundation: Use the simple form for ordinary possession, knowledge or belief: I have two sisters; We know the address; I believe the explanation. These describe conditions rather than actions unfolding before us. Merely adding at the moment does not make every state naturally progressive: I know the answer at the moment is ordinary English. The term stative is a useful tendency, not a permanent prohibition attached to a spelling. Compare We have a small kitchen, describing possession, with We are having lunch, describing an event. The verb is the same word, but its meaning and pattern change.
intermediate: Several familiar contrasts illustrate the importance of interpretation. I think the figures are wrong expresses an opinion; I am thinking about the figures describes a process of consideration. The soup tastes salty reports a perception; The cook is tasting the soup describes deliberate sampling. He is polite presents a characteristic; He is being unusually polite describes behaviour in the current situation. Progressive be is normally about conduct or a temporary presentation, not ordinary identity: She is being a dentist is not the normal way to state her profession. Read the complements and the situation before selecting a form.
advanced: Some predicates permit more flexibility than a short classroom list suggests. I feel tired and I am feeling tired can both describe a current condition, with the progressive making its present or temporary character more prominent. Informal I am loving this concert presents enjoyment as an immediate experience; it is marked by context and register rather than automatically ungrammatical. Repeated brief events can also receive progressive interpretation: Someone has been tapping on the window. A progressive with always can express an evaluative view of repeated behaviour, as in He is always interrupting, without making annoyance an obligatory part of the grammar.
expert: Temporary does not define progressive, and permanent does not define simple. We are currently living with relatives can be progressive without a promise that the arrangement will soon end; I live with relatives is a neutral characterisation, even when the arrangement is temporary. A speaker chooses how to package the situation. Duration is another independent property: I have known her for thirty years is lengthy but normally simple. Where a creative advertisement or a special discourse uses a normally stative verb progressively, identify the intended interpretation and register. Do not extend that exceptional use to every context, and do not reject it solely because a memorised list says never.

patterns.meaning: Possession or another stative relationship, according to the noun and context.
A dynamic interpretation such as experiencing, considering or deliberately sampling.

examples.analysis: Weighs expresses a measured property; simple is ordinary.

examples.sentence: The assistant is weighing the parcel.
examples.analysis: Weighing describes an action performed on the parcel.

examples.sentence: I have been thinking about your suggestion, although I still think it needs revision.
examples.analysis: Thinking is a process; think expresses the opinion reached or held.

contrasts.note: Both are grammatical: a characterisation contrasts with behaviour in the relevant situation.

exceptions: Some expressions allow simple and progressive state-like readings: I feel better and I am feeling better are both established. A learner should explain the viewpoint rather than force a universal ban.

mistakes.problem: I am knowing the password, in an ordinary statement of current knowledge.
mistakes.reason: Ordinary know in this sense is stative and normally uses a simple construction.

mistakes.problem: The owner is having three warehouses, meaning possession.
mistakes.reason: Possession normally takes simple have. Having may be progressive in event meanings such as having a meeting.

glossary.definition: A reading that presents a condition, perception, possession or relationship rather than an unfolding action.
A reading that presents action, development or change.
glossary.example: The surveyor is measuring the flat describes an activity.

modules.title: Duration, starting points and temporal endpoints
modules.definition: For normally introduces a duration, since a starting point in temporal uses, by a latest time or deadline, and until the endpoint of a continuing situation. These meanings guide interpretation but do not select one tense mechanically.
foundation: A duration answers How long? Use for with a measured interval: for twenty minutes, for a decade, for several weeks. A temporal starting point answers From when? Use since with a point or a clause locating that point: since Tuesday; since the office moved. Compare We have waited for an hour and We have waited since nine. Both can describe waiting that began earlier and continues now. Do not replace for with since merely because the sentence contains a perfect construction. The complement after the preposition determines which expression accurately represents the intended interval.
intermediate: For works with past, present and future reference: We waited for an hour yesterday; We have waited for an hour; We will stay for an hour. Since often combines with perfect constructions when measuring from an earlier point to a later viewpoint, but it is not exclusively a present-perfect signal. By 2022, she had worked here for five years is a past-perfect account, and She had been unwell since Monday measures to a past reference point. Since can also mean because: Since the gate was locked, we used another entrance gives a reason, not the beginning of a duration.
advanced: By sets a latest acceptable or relevant time: Send the signed form by Friday means no later than Friday. Until presents continuation to an endpoint: Keep the original until Friday means retain it through the relevant interval. Negation changes the relationship: She did not sign until Friday locates the eventual signing no earlier than Friday in the ordinary reading. Compare She had signed by Friday, which presents signing as achieved at or before that point. These are not stylistic substitutes. Preserve the intended deadline, continuation or delay when correcting a sentence, and do not change a promise into a mere prediction.
expert: The temporal expression and the verb viewpoint contribute separate information. By six, I will have finished explicitly looks back from a future boundary; I will finish by six can communicate the same deadline without a perfect form. A finished date is compatible with past perfect when another past viewpoint is established: At the review in May, we discovered that the permit had expired in March. The finished-time restriction on ordinary present perfect does not ban past perfect with dates. Until and by can also have non-temporal uses, and temporal clauses require their own analysis. Describe the particular construction rather than converting a useful contrast into an unrestricted word-substitution rule.

patterns.meaning: Measure an interval or locate its beginning.

patterns.form: by + deadline; continuing situation + until + endpoint
patterns.meaning: Distinguish completion no later than a time from continuation up to a time.

examples.sentence: The exhibition remained open until six.
examples.analysis: Remaining open continues to the stated endpoint.

examples.sentence: The driver must return the vehicle by six.
examples.analysis: The return is due no later than the deadline.

examples.sentence: By last winter, the family had lived there for a decade.
examples.analysis: A past viewpoint licenses a past perfect with a duration; no present continuation is asserted.

contrasts.note: Both are grammatical. Work continues to the endpoint in A; completion occurs no later than the deadline in B.

exceptions: Since is not always temporal: Since you have the key, please open the cabinet means because. Its presence does not itself require a perfect construction in every clause.

mistakes.problem: The queue has stretched outside since two hours.
mistakes.repair: The queue has stretched outside for two hours.
mistakes.reason: Two hours is a duration, not a starting point.

mistakes.problem: The customer has waited for Monday; intended meaning: the waiting began on Monday.
mistakes.repair: The customer has waited since Monday.
mistakes.reason: Use since to identify the intended starting point. Wait for Monday has a different meaning: await that day.

glossary.definition: The length of time for which a situation holds or an event continues.
The latest time allowed for an action or result.
glossary.example: Submit by noon gives a deadline.

modules.title: Already, yet, just, lately and recently in context
modules.definition: Time adverbs help locate events and convey expectations. Their meaning, position and compatibility with a construction must be interpreted together; they are not automatic tense selectors.
foundation: Already commonly presents a situation as existing or achieved by a relevant point, often earlier than expected: The bus has already left. Yet in a question asks whether an expected event has happened by now: Has the bus left yet? In a negative, The bus has not left yet indicates that departure has not happened up to the reference point and commonly remains expected. Just can mean a very short time ago: The bus has just left. These adverbs add interpretation to the clause; the verb form still needs to fit the broader temporal setting.
intermediate: Position changes emphasis and can affect naturalness. Already and recent-event just commonly follow the first auxiliary: We have already checked the locks; We had just finished. Already can also appear at the end: Have you finished already? often expresses surprise. Yet commonly appears at the end of a question or negative statement. It also has other established uses: a yet more difficult problem means a still more difficult one, while The result is promising yet uncertain uses yet as a coordinator. Identify the use before applying a rule learned for temporal questions.
advanced: Lately normally refers to a recent interval, especially with states, repeated events or continuing activity: I have been sleeping badly lately. Recently can do that too, but also readily locates a single completed past event: We inspected the lift recently. A precise finished time such as last Tuesday normally selects a past construction for the event: We inspected it last Tuesday. British English frequently uses present perfect for recent events with just, already and yet; American English also commonly uses simple past in such contexts: Did you send it yet? This is an established regional alternative, not evidence of carelessness.
expert: Adverbs carry scope and pragmatic expectations as well as clock time. Just may mean only, exactly, or emphatic merely, so I just need a signature need not describe a very recent need. Already does not require perfect aspect: We already know the answer is simple present. Special contexts permit negated already, for example a question challenging a presupposition, so not usually is more accurate than never. An assessment must give sufficient context when two tense-aspect forms or adverb positions remain defensible. Where the task asks for the most natural expression in a stated register, explain that criterion rather than marking every less frequent alternative as structurally impossible.

patterns.meaning: Common position for already and recent-event just with a perfect auxiliary.
Common temporal use concerning an expected event up to the relevant point.

examples.sentence: The catering team has already prepared the room.
examples.analysis: Already indicates completion by now, perhaps earlier than expected.

examples.sentence: Has the repair team tested the alarm yet?
examples.analysis: Yet asks whether the expected test has occurred up to now.

examples.sentence: The manager recently visited the site, but maintenance has been irregular lately.
examples.analysis: Recently locates one visit; lately frames a recent interval of maintenance.

contrasts.a: I have just called the laboratory.
contrasts.note: Both can report a recent call. The perfect is frequent in British English; simple past is also an established American English choice when no finished date is stated.

exceptions: These words have other senses and constructions: yet can mean nevertheless or still in combinations, and just can mean only. Analyse the actual use instead of applying a tense rule to the spelling alone.

mistakes.problem: She has already sent the application yet, meaning it is complete.
mistakes.repair: She has already sent the application.
mistakes.reason: Ordinary affirmative completion uses already; temporal yet does not naturally add this meaning at the end.

mistakes.problem: They have just wrote to the supplier.
mistakes.repair: They have just written to the supplier.
mistakes.reason: The perfect auxiliary requires written; just does not alter the required verb form.

glossary.definition: An adverb that contributes information about time or temporal relationships.
glossary.example: Recently locates an event in a recent period.

glossary.definition: The portion of an expression over which a word’s meaning operates.
glossary.example: Just in I just need help can limit what is needed rather than locate the need in time.

questions.prompt: Which construction is perfect progressive?
questions.why: Has is finite perfect have; been is the participle of be; checking is the progressive -ing form.

questions.prompt: What does I have been repairing the clock normally leave open without more context?
options: Whether the construction contains a perfect auxiliary
Whether the clock is now completely repaired
Whether the speaker is the subject
questions.why: The construction asserts recent repair activity but does not guarantee completion. The other properties are expressed in the sentence.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses have with its ordinary possession meaning?
options: We are having the windows replaced.
questions.why: Have three storage rooms expresses possession; the others describe events or a causative arrangement.

questions.prompt: The chef is tasting the sauce. Which analysis is accurate?
options: The sentence asserts that the sauce tastes pleasant.
Is is a perfect auxiliary here.
Tasting describes deliberate sampling, a dynamic interpretation.
questions.why: The chef deliberately samples the sauce; the progressive is natural in this action meaning. No judgement of pleasantness is asserted.

questions.prompt: The archive has been closed ____ last Wednesday. Choose the expression that identifies the starting point.
questions.why: Since last Wednesday identifies when the interval began. For needs a duration; during locates within an interval; until gives an endpoint.

questions.prompt: The archive was closed ____ three weeks and reopened yesterday.
questions.why: For three weeks measures a duration in a completed past situation. For does not require present perfect.

questions.prompt: Which instruction sets a one-off submission deadline no later than Friday?
options: Wait for the form since Friday.
Submit the form for Friday, meaning the submission began Friday.
questions.why: By Friday supplies the required deadline. Until concerns continuation; the other phrases do not express the stated relationship.

questions.prompt: Which observation accurately compares common British and American usage for a recent event?
options: British English often uses I have just sent it; American English also commonly uses I just sent it.
American English has no present perfect.
British English always forbids simple past.
questions.why: Both are established; the comparison concerns a frequent regional choice, not the elimination of a tense from either variety.

questions.prompt: Review for neutral formal English: During the last hour, Mira has been checking the sensors. Which judgement is defensible?
options: Replace checking with checked while keeping all other words.
No error: the perfect progressive naturally presents the recent checking activity.
questions.why: During the last hour is a valid interval; Mira selects has; been checking is an active progressive. None of the proposed changes is required.

questions.prompt: Which statement gives a reliable distinction between lately and recently?
options: Lately normally frames a recent interval; recently also readily locates a single past event.
Recently requires a progressive in every clause.
Lately means arriving after the scheduled time.
Both words always make a present-perfect answer uniquely necessary.
questions.why: Lately is associated with a recent interval, not lateness. Neither word mechanically selects one tense-aspect construction.

questions.prompt: Classify the auxiliary sequence in The staff had been monitoring the tunnel. Identify the finite form and the two participial forms.
questions.model: Had is finite past perfect have; been is the past participle of be; monitoring is the -ing form in the progressive construction.
rubric: Identify had as the finite element.
Distinguish the role of been from the lexical monitoring.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between I have painted the door and I have been painting the door. Do not claim that both guarantee completion.
questions.model: The first normally presents the door-painting as completed and relevant now. The second foregrounds the recent activity and leaves completion to context.
rubric: Distinguish completion from activity focus.
State that the progressive does not itself establish a finished door.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Complete the explicit perfect-progressive sequences using check: The researchers have ____ ____ the samples; by yesterday evening they had ____ ____ them for a week.
questions.model: The researchers have been checking the samples; by yesterday evening they had been checking them for a week.
rubric: Use been followed by checking in both gaps.
Keep have versus had consistent with the stated reference points.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Can The engine has been stopping unexpectedly describe grammatical English? Explain a plausible reading.
questions.model: Yes. It can describe repeated brief failures over a recent interval; stopping is interpreted iteratively rather than as one stop lasting indefinitely.
rubric: Supply a repeated-event interpretation.
Do not use an absolute ban based solely on the verb stop.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Give the meanings of I think the route is safe and I am thinking about the route.
questions.model: The first states an opinion. The second describes consideration of the route as an activity.
rubric: Identify opinion versus mental process.
Do not imply that progressive thinking has the same complement pattern as opinion think.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: For ordinary possession, complete with the appropriate form of own: This charity ____ the building, and it has done so since 1998.
questions.model: This charity owns the building, and it has done so since 1998.
rubric: Use simple owns for ordinary possession.
Keep singular agreement with charity when treated as a single owner.
alternatives: This charity has owned the building since 1998 is a grammatical reformulation.

questions.prompt: Explain why The parcel weighs ten kilos and The clerk is weighing the parcel use different forms of weigh.
questions.model: The first presents a measured property; the second presents deliberate measurement as an activity.
rubric: Differentiate stative property and dynamic action.
Identify the progressive auxiliary is in the second sentence.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Is I am feeling better necessarily wrong because feel can describe a state? Give a qualified explanation.
questions.model: No. Feel allows ordinary simple and progressive readings here. I feel better characterises the condition; I am feeling better draws attention to the current experience or development.
rubric: Accept the established progressive use.
Explain viewpoint rather than inventing a permanent/temporary law.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Choose for or since: We had been waiting ____ forty minutes when the office opened.
questions.model: We had been waiting for forty minutes when the office opened.
rubric: Identify forty minutes as duration.
Retain the past reference rather than unnecessarily replacing had with have.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Explain the practical difference between Keep the backup until Monday and Finish the backup by Monday.
questions.model: The first instructs retention through an interval ending Monday; the second sets a completion deadline no later than Monday.
rubric: Distinguish continuation and deadline.
Do not treat until and by as synonyms.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Combine these facts with since: The workshop moved in 2020. It has occupied the present building continuously from that point to now.
questions.model: The workshop has occupied the present building since it moved in 2020.
rubric: Make the starting event a since-clause.
Use a construction that retains continuity to now.
alternatives: The workshop has occupied the present building since 2020.

questions.prompt: At an audit in July, the investigator said The licence had expired in March. Does in March make the past perfect impossible? Explain.
questions.model: No. March is earlier than the established July viewpoint. A finished date is compatible with past perfect; the usual restriction concerns ordinary present perfect combined with a finished event time.
rubric: Identify July as the later past viewpoint.
Distinguish past perfect from present perfect.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Arrange these words into a neutral sentence: already / have / the technicians / checked / the wiring.
questions.model: The technicians have already checked the wiring.
rubric: Place already naturally after the first auxiliary.
Keep have followed by checked.
alternatives: The technicians have checked the wiring already.

questions.prompt: Compare Has the letter arrived yet? and Has the letter arrived already?
questions.model: Yet neutrally asks whether the expected arrival has happened by now. Already can express surprise that arrival has happened so soon; intonation and context affect that implication.
rubric: Explain the expectation difference.
Avoid claiming surprise is mechanically obligatory in every already-question.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: In I just need the account number, give a plausible meaning of just that is not temporal.
questions.model: Just can mean only: the account number is all that is needed.
rubric: Identify a limiting rather than recent-time meaning.
Keep the intended scope over the required information.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Edit only genuine faults: We have just wrote the summary. The director already knows the outcome. We have not sent the annex yet.
questions.model: We have just written the summary. The director already knows the outcome. We have not sent the annex yet.
rubric: Repair wrote to the past participle written.
Retain simple already knows and negative sent … yet as valid.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Explain why I have worked here for five years and I have been working here for five years may both be defensible in the same continuing-employment context.
questions.model: Both can cover employment beginning five years ago and continuing now. The simple gives a neutral statement of the period; the progressive gives greater attention to the continuing course of activity. Neither ending forces a different number of years.
rubric: Recognise that both forms can be grammatical.
Describe a viewpoint difference without fabricating a different duration.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

questions.prompt: Write two sentences using by and until about the same conference, one giving a deadline and one requiring continuation.
questions.model: Send the programme by Thursday. Keep the registration desk open until six on Friday.
rubric: Use by for an explicit deadline.
Use until with a situation that can continue through an interval.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

corrections.prompt: Correct: The volunteers have been collected the forms all afternoon.
corrections.model: The volunteers have been collecting the forms all afternoon.
rubric: Use the -ing form after progressive been.
Preserve the active volunteers as the collectors.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

corrections.prompt: Correct the ordinary possession statement: My cousin is having two motorcycles.
rubric: Use simple have for the intended possession.
Retain the stated quantity.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

corrections.prompt: Correct: The lift has been out of service since three days.
corrections.model: The lift has been out of service for three days.
rubric: Change since to for before a duration.
Keep the continuing relevant state.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

corrections.prompt: Correct without changing the intended starting point: We have worked here for March 2021.
corrections.model: We have worked here since March 2021.
rubric: Use since with the starting date.
Do not replace the date with an invented duration.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

corrections.prompt: Revise to neutral ordinary word order, keeping the same meaning: Have the engineers tested already the alarm?
corrections.model: Have the engineers already tested the alarm?
rubric: Avoid ordinary already placement between tested and its direct object.
Retain the question’s perfect auxiliary.
alternatives: Have the engineers tested the alarm already?

corrections.prompt: Correct the participle: The committee had just chose its chair when the fire alarm sounded.
corrections.model: The committee had just chosen its chair when the fire alarm sounded.
rubric: Use chosen after had.
Retain the earlier-past relationship.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

corrections.prompt: Decide whether a change is required: The chef has been tasting the sauces to compare their seasoning.
corrections.model: No change is required. Tasting describes deliberate repeated sampling, so the perfect progressive is natural.
rubric: Recognise the dynamic meaning.
Do not replace a valid progressive merely because taste appears on some stative-verb lists.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

corrections.prompt: Decide whether the tense must change: By the 2023 review, the charity had used the old building for twenty years.
corrections.model: No change is required. The past perfect relates twenty years of use to the later past review.
rubric: Keep the legitimate past reference point.
Do not interpret for as an automatic present-perfect signal.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

transformations.prompt: The evidence says that repairs occupied the previous two hours; it does not establish completion. Rewrite as a present perfect progressive sentence about the crew.
transformations.model: The crew has been carrying out repairs for the last two hours.
rubric: Use have/has been plus -ing.
Do not add a claim that the repairs are complete.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

transformations.prompt: Rewrite without until while preserving the no-earlier-than meaning: The office did not release the result until Tuesday.
transformations.model: The office released the result on Tuesday, not before then.
rubric: Preserve the eventual release on Tuesday and the absence of an earlier release.
Avoid by Tuesday, which changes the temporal condition.
alternatives: The result was released on Tuesday, not earlier.

writing.prompt: Write an 80–120-word maintenance update. Distinguish one completed repair, one ongoing or recently stopped activity, a duration, a starting point and a deadline. Do not claim completion where evidence only shows activity.
writing.model: The team has replaced the damaged fuse, and the lights now work. The technicians have been checking the remaining circuits for two hours, although their inspection is not complete. The emergency entrance has remained open since nine. We have already informed the building manager, but we have not received the replacement sensor yet. Please send the access log by noon tomorrow and keep the temporary signs in place until the manager confirms that the inspection is finished. The report will distinguish completed repairs from work still requiring verification.
rubric: Use an appropriate completed-event perfect and an activity-focused perfect progressive.
Use for and since according to duration and starting point.
Separate by-deadline from until-continuation.
Preserve uncertainty about unfinished work and review adverb placement.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 1: In The courier has been waiting outside, identify the whole subject and the finite auxiliary.
recall.model: The courier is the subject noun phrase; has is the finite auxiliary.
rubric: Name the complete subject, not only its head.
Identify has rather than waiting as finite.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 6: Compare She checks the pump each morning and She is checking the pump now.
recall.model: The simple characterises a routine; the progressive presents activity in progress at the relevant moment.
rubric: Relate each form to its stated context.
Do not define simple as permanent.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 7: In The guests had left before we arrived, which event is presented as earlier? Is before itself compatible with past simple in another defensible account?
recall.model: The guests’ leaving is presented as earlier. Before can also make order clear in The guests left before we arrived; past perfect is not mechanically required whenever before occurs.
rubric: Identify the earlier leaving.
Recognise that explicit sequencing can permit a simple-past alternative.
alternatives: Accept other grammatical responses that preserve the stated facts, viewpoint and relevant distinction.
